slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter two: the examination of motion.

slides.heading: Where is the moving?
points: Walk across a room: you, the walking, the floor
Is the moving in the part crossed, or not yet crossed?
Who is the walker, apart from the walking?
slides.say: Walk across a room. Nothing seems simpler. There is you, there is the walking, and there is the floor you cross. You were at the door, and now you are at the window. The second chapter asks where, in that plain event, the moving is actually found. Is it in the part of the floor already crossed? In the part not yet crossed? In the spot under your foot right now? And who is the walker, apart from the walking?

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Chapter 1 tested causes; chapter 2 tests motion
Done, not yet done, being done
Is the doer the same as the deed, or different?
slides.say: Chapter one tested causes, the way one thing is supposed to bring about another. Chapter two turns to motion, the most vivid kind of change. It uses a pattern of analysis that Nagarjuna will use again and again: divide the field into the done, the not yet done and the being done, and look for the event in each. It also gives the classic test of agent and action: is the doer the same as the deed, or different?

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Twenty-five verses
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: Where is the moving?
points: Already crossed: the moving there is over
Not yet crossed: the moving has not begun
Being crossed: is there such a strip?
slides.say: Now the explanation. The chapter opens with a simple division, in verse two point one. Take the path of any movement, say your walk from the door to the window. At any moment the path falls into three parts. There is the stretch already crossed. There is the stretch not yet crossed. And there is, it seems, the stretch being crossed now. If motion is really happening, it must be happening in one of these. It is not in the stretch already crossed. That part is finished; the moving there is over. It is not in the stretch not yet crossed. The moving there has not begun.

slides.heading: Three parts of a path
slides.say: So it must be in the third part, the stretch being crossed. But look for that stretch. Wherever you draw the line, the floor divides into what is behind the foot and what is ahead of it. The now of the step has no width of its own. Take away the crossed and the not crossed, and no third strip is left over for the moving to live in. That is what the diagram shows: two parts ruled out at once, and the third with no extent of its own.

slides.heading: Two goings, two goers
slides.say: The opponent replies, in verse two point two, that the movement of the feet is clearly happening, and not behind you or ahead of you. So going must be in the place being gone over. Nagarjuna's answer is subtle. What makes a stretch of floor the place being gone over? Only the going happening on it. Without a going, it is just floor. So the name already contains a going. Now the opponent says the going is in that place. Then there are two goings: the one that made the place count as being gone over, and the one now said to happen in it. If he denies the first, he has a place being gone over that nothing is going over. And if he accepts both, a going needs a goer, so two goings need two goers. One person crossing a room has become two.

slides.heading: The cup is made of the water
points: We picture going as a thing sitting somewhere
But the place is defined by the going
You cannot put the going into the place
slides.say: This sounds like word-play, but it exposes a real habit. We picture the going as a thing sitting somewhere, like water in a cup. Nagarjuna shows that the cup, the place being gone over, is itself made of the water, the going. You cannot put the going into the place, because without the going there is no such place to put it in.

slides.heading: Who goes?
points: Not a goer: that says the going twice
Not a non-goer: he does not go
No third kind of person between the two
slides.say: The same pattern is applied to the person, in verses eight to eleven. Who is it that goes? Not a goer: someone already counted as a goer is already going, so the goer goes says the going twice. Not a non-goer: someone who is not going does not go. And there is no third kind of person between the two. If you insist on a goer who then goes, you must first have a goer without going, which is not a goer. The point is not that no one walks. It is that walker and walking are not two items, one of which picks up the other. Our grammar, subject then verb, makes it look as if a walker stood ready and then started to walk. Look for that ready walker, and you find only someone already walking, or someone not walking at all.

slides.heading: Starting and stopping
points: Going does not begin in any part of the path
Stopping meets the same fate
Lift a cup: when did the lifting start?
slides.say: If motion really happened, it would have to start somewhere. Where does going begin? Not on the stretch already gone over, for there it has already happened. Not on the stretch not yet gone over, for nothing is going on there. Not on the stretch being gone over, for that already has going in it. Stopping meets the same fate. A goer does not stop, since a goer is one who is going, and a non-goer was not going. Try it in slow motion. Lift a cup from the table. When did the lifting start? At every instant you choose, either the lifting is already under way, or it is not yet happening. The moment of starting, taken as a thing of its own, is not found. Yet the cup is lifted.

slides.heading: Same or different?
slides.say: Verses eighteen to twenty-one give one of the most important tests in the whole text. If walker and walking were real things, each with its own nature, they would have to be either the same thing or two different things. If they were the same, doer and deed would be one, and it would make as much sense to say the walking walks. If they were different, each could exist without the other: a walker who is never walking, and a walking with no one doing it. Neither is ever met. Something that can be established neither as one with its partner nor as different from it cannot be established as a thing at all. Fire and fuel, agent and action, and the self and its parts will all be tested the same way.

slides.heading: Existent, non-existent or both
points: An existing goer needs no going
A non-existing goer goes nowhere
Not found is not the same as does not happen
slides.say: The chapter ends with the four-cornered pattern met in chapter one. A goer who already exists, complete, does not need to go. A goer who does not exist goes nowhere. One who both exists and does not exist has both problems. So going, goer and the place to be gone are not found. Not found is the key phrase. Nagarjuna is not saying, as Zeno was taken to say, that motion is an illusion and the arrow never flies. His analysis shows something narrower: that motion is not found as a thing of its own, located in a strip of path, carried by a walker who stands apart from it. In the reading of Chandrakirti and Tsongkhapa, what is refuted is going established by its own nature, not the going that the world sees.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: You still walk to the window, and get there
Walker, walking and path designated together
None stands first, waiting for the others
slides.say: You still walk to the window, and you get there. Trains run to timetables, and the timetable is right. What the chapter removes is the picture behind the words: a self-standing walker carrying a self-standing walking across a self-standing floor. What remains is walking, met without those three pieces. The walker is called a walker because of the walking; the walking is a walking because someone is walking somewhere; the path is a path because it is walked. None stands first, waiting for the others to arrive.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Feel the walking itself
Look for a walker standing behind it
Nothing is missing
slides.say: Try it the next time you walk. Feel the walking itself: the shift of weight, the floor arriving under the foot, the room sliding past. Look for a walker standing behind it, steering. The walking is vivid and exact. The walker, as something apart from it, is not found. Nothing is missing.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: the Interlude
The Logic of Dependency (bonus article)
Anatta to Emptiness: Observer, Chariot, Appendix
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, the Interlude, on motion and the mover. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, on change without a changer. And in The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, the chapters on the collapse of the observer and the chariot, and the appendix on why grammar keeps building a mover. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter three, the examination of the senses.
